# QuickOper

> Verified-calculation tools for personal money decisions. Every calculation runs
> entirely in the visitor's browser; no input is transmitted, logged or stored.

QuickOper computes, it does not advise. Each tool performs deterministic
arithmetic and publishes its formula, its intermediate values, a full
period-by-period schedule, and the fixture tests proving its output matches a
real published third-party figure.

Nothing on this site is financial, tax or investment advice. The expertise
claimed is computational, not advisory.

## Tools

### Debt payoff calculator — avalanche vs snowball
URL: https://quickoper.com/finance/debt-payoff-calculator
Computes: months to debt freedom and total interest, for the avalanche and
snowball strategies and for a minimum-payments-only baseline, with a full
month-by-month schedule.
Inputs: per-debt balance, annual rate and minimum payment; one total monthly
payment.
Jurisdiction: none. Interest is charged monthly on the opening balance, which
is a convention, not a rule of any one country.
Methodology: https://quickoper.com/methodology
Verification: https://quickoper.com/verify

### Coast FIRE calculator
URL: https://quickoper.com/finance/coast-fire-calculator
Computes: the amount that must already be invested for it to reach a retirement
target with no further contributions, plus a year-by-year projection.
Inputs: current age, retirement age, amount invested, annual spending,
withdrawal rate, real annual return, monthly contribution.
Jurisdiction: none. No tax treatment or account type is modelled.
Methodology: https://quickoper.com/methodology
Verification: https://quickoper.com/verify

### Mortgage overpayment calculator
URL: https://quickoper.com/finance/mortgage-overpayment-calculator
Computes: what an extra monthly payment removes from a fixed-rate mortgage, in
months and in interest, with the full month-by-month amortisation schedule.
Inputs: amount borrowed, annual interest rate, term in years, extra paid monthly.
Jurisdiction: US fixed-rate convention. Interest is charged monthly at
annualRate/12, which is how a lender's nominal APR is defined.
Key figures, computed on $320,000 at 6.706% over 30 years:
  - Required monthly payment: $2,066.16. This matches calculator.net's
    published output for the same inputs, to the cent.
  - Contractual schedule: 360 payments, $423,821.51 of interest.
  - Paying $200 extra a month: 280 payments, $312,930.95 of interest.
  - That removes 80 months and $110,890.56 of interest.
  - Month 1 on the contractual payment: $1,788.27 interest, $277.89 principal.
  - The final payment is $2,070.07, larger than the others, because a payment
    rounded to the cent leaves a residue that lenders collect in the last month
    rather than issuing a 361st bill.
Not modelled: escrow, PMI, fees, prepayment penalties, adjustable rates.
Methodology: https://quickoper.com/methodology
Verification: https://quickoper.com/verify

## Derivations

### How long minimum payments take, and when they never finish
URL: https://quickoper.com/minimum-payments
States: a minimum payment reduces a credit card balance only if it is larger
than that month's interest. Interest is balance x (APR / 12); the balance moves
by (interest - payment). If the payment is smaller than the interest the balance
rises every month and the card never clears, regardless of how long payments
continue. There is no third case.
Key figures, all computed at build time by the same engine the debt payoff
calculator runs, assuming a fixed monthly payment and no further spending:
  - $3,000 at 29.99% APR charges $74.98 of interest in month one. A $30
    payment leaves the balance $44.98 HIGHER than before it. The card never
    reaches zero.
  - The stand-still payment - the amount that holds a balance exactly level and
    repays nothing - is balance x (APR / 12). On $3,000 at 29.99% that is
    $74.98 a month.
  - $3,000 at 29.99% paying $90 a month clears in 73 months and costs
    $3,526.99 of interest, which is $526.99 MORE than the balance itself.
  - $6,000 at 22.99% paying $150 a month clears in 77 months, costing
    $5,492.03 of interest.
  - The same $6,000 at $250 a month clears in 33 months, costing $2,113.21.
    An extra $100 a month removes 44 months and $3,378.82 of interest.
  - These are the OPTIMISTIC figures. Issuers commonly set the minimum as a
    percentage of the balance, which shrinks as the balance falls, so a real
    minimum payment takes longer than a fixed payment of the same starting
    amount.

### How credit card interest is actually calculated
URL: https://quickoper.com/credit-card-interest
States: a credit card daily periodic rate is APR divided by 365. At 22.99% APR
that is 0.062986% per day. Interest is charged on the average daily balance of
the billing cycle, not the closing balance.
Key figures, all computed on a $6,000 balance at 22.99% APR:
  - 28-day cycle: $105.82. 30-day cycle: $113.38. 31-day cycle: $117.15.
  - APR/12 monthly approximation: $114.95 per month.
  - Over a full year both methods total exactly $1,379.40.
  - With daily compounding, one year costs $1,550.30 - an effective annual
    rate of 25.838% against a stated 22.99%.
  - A $200 payment on a 30-day cycle costs $109.60 of interest if it lands on
    day 1 and $113.25 if it lands on day 30.

### Why a 7% return is not 0.583% a month
URL: https://quickoper.com/monthly-return-rate
States: converting a stated annual RETURN to a monthly rate requires the twelfth
root, not division by twelve. A 7% annual return is 0.565415% per month, being
(1.07)^(1/12) - 1. Dividing gives 0.583333%, which compounds to an effective
7.2290% per year rather than 7%.
Key figures:
  - $100,000 for 30 years at a stated 7%: $761,225.50 using the twelfth root,
    $811,649.75 using r/12. The error overstates by $50,424.24, or 6.62%.
  - The error is always in the flattering direction.
  - An APR is the exception: a lender APR is a nominal rate defined as twelve
    times the monthly rate, so dividing by twelve is correct for debt.
  - Real return is nominal divided by inflation, not minus: 8% nominal against
    3% inflation is (1.08/1.03)-1 = 4.854369%, not 5%. Over 30 years on
    $100,000 that is $414,568.14 against $432,194.24.

### Where the 4% rule comes from, and what it does not say
URL: https://quickoper.com/withdrawal-rate
States: a withdrawal rate converts annual spending into a savings target by
dividing 100 by the rate. 4% is 25 times spending; 3% is 33.33 times.
Key figures, computed on $40,000 of annual spending:
  - 4% -> $1,000,000. 3.5% -> $1,142,857.14. 3% -> $1,333,333.33.
  - Moving from 4% to 3% adds 8.33x spending, a 33.3% increase in capital,
    because the multiple is 1/rate and therefore a hyperbola.
  - Bengen (1994) tested 30-year windows in US market history. The finding was
    never tested for longer retirements, other markets, or after fees and tax.
  - Sequence-of-returns risk, demonstrated: the same ten annual returns applied
    in opposite orders to a $1,000,000 portfolio drawing $40,000 a year end
    $1,573,834.11 (bad years first) against $1,835,954.59 (good years first) -
    $262,120.48 apart on an identical 10% arithmetic mean.

### What a coast number is, and what it is not
URL: https://quickoper.com/coast-number
States: a coast number is target / (1 + real return)^years - the amount that must
already be invested for compounding alone to reach a retirement target with no
further contributions. Passing it makes further SAVING optional, not working.
Key figures, on a $1,000,000 target:
  - At 5% real: 40 years out $142,045.68; 30 years $231,377.45; 20 years
    $376,889.48; 10 years $613,913.25; 5 years $783,526.17.
  - Sensitivity to the assumed return, 30 years out: 7% gives $131,367.12,
    5% gives $231,377.45, 3% gives $411,986.76. The pessimistic assumption
    needs more than three times the capital of the optimistic one.
  - The return must be a REAL return if the target is in today's money.
  - It cannot express sequence-of-returns risk; it is a single discount at a
    constant rate.
